#1912. AZ Alkmaar vs Groningen - prediction, team news, lineups

By Nsidibe Akpan | 06 Nov 2026 23:38

AZ Alkmaar are in a poor run in the league and will hope to turn things around when they host FC Groningen in the Eredivisie at the AFAS Stadion on Sunday.

Sitting fifth in the Eredivisie table, AZ have lost three in a row in all competitions and taken one point from their last four league games, but eighth-placed Groningen have conceded 12 goals in three games against the current top four, which hands the Cheese Farmers a real chance to end their slump.

Leeroy Echteld’s side lost 2-0 to Twente on October 25, 1-0 at Ajax on October 31 and 2-1 to Juventus on November 5, and their only goal in those three games was Mexx Meerdink’s 88th-minute finish in the Europa League.

The Ajax defeat came despite 20 shots to nine and 2.30 expected goals to 0.72, and Echteld said AZ’s data has never been this strong while the games against Feyenoord, Twente, Ajax and Juventus have brought no points.

Both Juventus goals followed AZ errors, as poor defending on the right let Randal Kolo Muani escape before Teun Koopmeiners’s 19th-minute strike and Mees de Wit lost the ball before Kolo Muani scored on 37 minutes, ending AZ’s 17-match unbeaten run in European home games.

It is a sharp turn from August, when Echteld won the first Rinus Michels Coach of the Month award of the season after AZ became the only club to win all four league games, including a 4-1 win at Utrecht on August 15 and a 5-2 home win over Go Ahead Eagles on August 29.

AZ have conceded 13 league goals in 11 games, level with PSV Eindhoven, Ajax and Heerenveen and behind only Twente (10) and Feyenoord (12), but their 20 goals scored are six fewer than Groningen have managed.

On Friday, Echteld said AZ are close to the style he wants and called Groningen one of the hardest-running sides in the Eredivisie, while Ro-Zangelo Daal leads the hosts with five league goals.

Dick Lukkien’s side have lost three of their last four games in all competitions, the exception being a 2-2 draw at NEC on October 25 in which Brynjolfur Willumsson scored twice before the interval and the hosts replied through Clement Bischoff and Noe Lebreton.

A 2-0 home defeat to second-tier Emmen on October 29 ended their KNVB Cup run in the first round, with Jack Cooper-Love scoring in the 10th and 55th minutes against Lukkien’s former club.

Jacob Ondrejka scored after 17 seconds against Sparta Rotterdam on November 1, but Cedric Hatenboer and Milan Zonneveld turned the game around before Thom van Bergen levelled on 29 minutes, and substitute Andrej Kostic punished a mix-up between goalkeeper Etienne Vaessen and Hans Hateboer with an empty-net finish in the 85th minute.

Willumsson is level on eight league goals with Wout Weghorst and Soren Tengstedt at the top of the scoring charts, and Groningen’s 26 league goals are six more than AZ have scored.

The Pride of the North have taken one point from three games against the current top four, conceding five at PSV Eindhoven, two against Twente and five against Ajax, and 14 of their 15 league points have come against clubs in the bottom half.

Groningen beat AZ 3-0 at the Euroborg on March 22, 2026, through a Marvin Peersman penalty and goals from Van Bergen and Tygo Land, but they have lost all five of their visits to Alkmaar in all competitions since December 2021, the latest a 4-1 defeat on August 10, 2025.

Lewis Schouten is the main doubt after leaving the Juventus game with a hamstring injury in the first half, soon after Koopmeiners’s goal, with Wesley Hoedt taking his place.

Stije Resink, who joined from Groningen in the summer, is out with a serious knee injury and Echteld said he is not expected back before January, while Jizz Hornkamp and goalkeeper Jeroen Zoet are also listed as unavailable.

Kees Smit made his comeback from injury off the bench against Juventus, but Echteld said he could not yet start, which leaves Smit, the 35-year-old Jordy Clasie, who has said he finds his reserve role hard, and Elijah Dijkstra as options from the bench.

Meerdink, Calvin Stengs and Daal started in the front three against Juventus, and no AZ suspensions have been reported.

Groningen will be without forward Ryan Metu and midfielder Travis Hernes, who was operated on this week, while David van der Werff and Alvin Nordin are doubts.

Defenders Elvis van der Laan, 18, and Tyrique Mercera are back after recent injuries, and Lukkien otherwise has a fully available squad.

Lukkien used a 4-2-3-1 against Sparta, with Vaessen in goal, Hateboer, Thijmen Blokzijl, Marco Rente and Mark Csinger in defence, Pelle Clement and Tika de Jonge in midfield, and Willumsson supported by Jorg Schreuders, Van Bergen and Ondrejka.

Groningen have had a full week to recover from that defeat, against roughly 68 hours for AZ after Thursday’s 9pm local kick-off, and Lukkien said his squad recovered well.

De Busser; Kasius, Goes, Hoedt, De Wit; Kwakman, Byskov, Koopmeiners; Stengs, Meerdink, Daal

Vaessen; Hateboer, Blokzijl, Rente, Csinger; Clement, De Jonge, Schreuders, Van Bergen, Ondrejka; Willumsson

Groningen have taken one point and conceded 12 goals in three games against the current top four, which suits an AZ side that created 2.30 expected goals at Ajax without scoring and should find the space it was denied at the Johan Cruijff Arena.

Groningen have scored in nine of their last 10 games in all competitions, the exception being the cup defeat to Emmen, so Willumsson, who struck twice at NEC, and Van Bergen should find a way past an AZ back line that may be without Schouten.

The case for the visitors is the turnaround, with AZ playing 68 hours after Thursday’s defeat and Groningen having won 3-0 in March, but they have lost five straight visits to Alkmaar and taken 14 of their 15 points against bottom-half sides, so we expect AZ’s greater depth to prove decisive.

#1904. Hutchinson worryingly claims ‘a lot’ of Milan players ‘didn’t show that hunger’ in Ferencvaros loss

Omari Hutchinson has questioned the desire of some of the players in the AC Milan squad who are not playing regularly.

Milan sunk to perhaps their lowest point of Ruben Amorim’s tenure so far as they were beaten 2-0 by Ferencvaros. The away side were good value for the win, and it complicates the mission to get into the knockout stages of the Europa League given the current position outside the top 24.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Amorim did not hold back after the game, accusing his team of lacking heart and desire. It is a third defeat in four European games for the Rossoneri, which is far off the expectations of one of the supposed pre-tournament favourites.

Hutchinson was interviewed by CBS Sports Golazo at the end of last night’s game and he offered his thoughts on what was another rough night, with MilanNews relaying his words.

“I think we had a very slow start. I think we were mentally prepared: they showed us all the tactics, what we had to do and how to start.

“I think we’ve been having a lot of slow starts lately, and even though we came out with a slightly more positive attitude in the second half, today it just wasn’t enough.

“I don’t think we showed that hunger to get to the ball, to make an impact in front of goal. So yeah, it was all very, very slow.”

And what needs to be done in the next matches to improve your performance and your style of play?

“I just think we need to play like we did against Inter. You could feel the energy in the locker room; you could tell we wanted to win. I think we didn’t show much humility today.

“We didn’t want to… well, a lot of players who aren’t playing didn’t show that hunger to want a starting spot, and I think that wasn’t enough. I think we’ll have to start strong on Sunday and be really good with the ball.”

Will you be able to find the strength to climb the rankings?

“Yes, yes, I think the game isn’t over until we’re out, so we just have to keep focusing. Yes, we just have to improve. We have a good group, the staff always helps us, shows us what we have to do.

“And now I think it’s up to us. I think we let everyone down today and we have another game on Sunday, we have to focus on that and come out strong.”

#1902. Real Sociedad vs Rayo Vallecano - prediction, team news, lineups

By Ben Sully | 06 Nov 2026 23:47, Last updated: 07 Nov 2026 02:50

Real Sociedad will look to extend their three-game unbeaten home run when they take on Rayo Vallecano in Sunday's La Liga encounter at Anoeta.

The Basque side start the weekend in fifth spot in La Liga, while the visitors are sitting in 12th position in the standings.

Real Sociedad are sitting four points adrift of the top four after winning six, drawing one and losing four of their 11 league games this season.

La Real enjoyed a three-game winning run in the top flight until they were stopped in their tracks by a narrow 2-1 defeat against rivals Athletic Bilbao in last Sunday's Basque derby at San Mames.

Orri Oskarsson failed to find the net in his substitute appearance last weekend, but he was able to score his fourth goal in five games in Thursday's Europa League clash against Lyon at Anoeta.

However, his effort was cancelled out by Corentin Tolisso's second-half volley, forcing Pellegrino Matarazzo's side to settle for a point that leaves them in 20th place in the league phase.

The draw at least made it three consecutive home games without defeat, and they will now look to record a third consecutive league win in front of their supporters after beating Levante and Deportivo A Coruna in their last two La Liga outings at Anoeta.

If they are to take the spoils from Sunday's contest, La Real will need to beat Rayo for the first time since completing a league double in the 2022-23 campaign, which included a 2-1 victory on home turf.

Rayo enter the weekend with a two-point cushion to the bottom three after recording three wins, three draws and four defeats in their 10 La Liga outings this term.

Benat San Jose's side have proven to be a tough team to beat in recent times, having lost just one of their previous five league games (W2, D2).

Rayo made light work of last Saturday's meeting with Celta Vigo at Vallecas, where Jorge de Frutos netted a brace before Unai Lopez scored his first goal of the season to complete a resounding 3-0 victory.

San Jose would have been particularly pleased to end the wait for his first La Liga clean sheet since taking over the reins from Inigo Perez in the summer.

The Rayo boss will now be looking to clinch his first away league win in charge of the club after seeing his side take just two points from their opening five road trips.

The visitors can certainly take confidence from the fact they have won their last two away meetings with Real Sociedad as part of a six-game unbeaten run in head-to-head games at any venue.

Real Sociedad remain without long-term absentee Alvaro Odriozola, while Mamadou Sarr is a doubt after being withdrawn at half time on Thursday due to a calf issue.

Arsen Zakharyan is battling to prove his fitness in time for Sunday’s fixture after missing the last two matches through injury.

Captain Mikel Oyarzabal is expected to be available for selection despite finishing the midweek draw against Lyon with a back problem.

As for Rayo, they are unable to call upon midfielder Oscar Valentin and forward Alvaro Garcia, who are sidelined with knee and hamstring injuries respectively.

San Jose is also working without the services of Augusto Batalla, Kumbulla and Luiz Felipe, the latter of whom is a long-term absentee after suffering a serious knee injury last month.

The Rayo boss will at least welcome back Pathe Ciss from a one-match ban for an accumulation of yellow cards.

Remiro; Aramburu, Zubeldia, Martin, Gomez; Soler, Turrientes; Kubo, Sucic, Guedes; Oyarzabal

Audero; Ratiu, Lejeune, Mujaid, Pedrosa; Lopez, Ciss; De Frutos, Diaz, Tsitaishvili; Camello

While Real Sociedad have found life difficult in recent meetings with Rayo, they come into this one on the back of consecutive home wins, and we think they will make full use of home advantage to get the better of a Rayo side that has lost three of their five away league games this term.

#1898. St Mirren 0 Rangers 2: Winless away run ended with comfortable victory for Ibrox side

Rangers banished their recent away day blues with a solid 2-0 win over St Mirren in Paisley.

Draws against Dundee and Hearts in their last two William Hill Premiership games away from Ibrox had blemished the Gers’ focused title challenge, but Derek McInnes’s side were determined to leave The Marbill Coaches Stadium without a mark on them.

In-form striker Ryan Naderi scored with a soft penalty after 18 minutes before returning skipper Dan Neil added a second just after the hour mark with a deflected strike to extend the Light Blues’ unbeaten run in all competitions to 12 games.

Rangers moved to within one point of leaders Celtic having played the same number of fixtures, albeit the Hoops can can restore their four-point lead against Kilmarnock at Celtic Park on Sunday before the the international break gives the league another breather.

The unusual 8pm kick off on a Saturday night added atmosphere to the evening. St Mirren boss Craig McLeish made five changes, with Declan John, Louis Jackson, Samuel Ramos, Ismeal Kabia and Jake Young all coming in while Neil replaced Tuur Rommens and James Penrice dropped to left-back.

Amid a hurly-burly start to the game, Buddies keeper Jacob Chapman saved an early effort from Rangers wide-man Badredine Bouananai, then in the 12th minute made a crucial block from Naderi, who latched on to a Kevin Kelsy header, at the expense of a corner which came to nothing.

However, the big striker soon made amends.

Back-tracking St Mirren attacker Ramos was far from happy when referee Nick Walsh pointed to the spot following his challenge on Penrice just inside the box, after the Gers defender had raced 60 yards to back up the Light Blues’ South Korea international attacker Kim Min-su.

It looked like there had been little contact but a VAR check confirmed the penalty and Naderi, with a stuttering run up, casually sent Chapman the wrong way with his spot-kick for his ninth goal of the season.

The aggrieved home side fought furiously to get back on level terms and on a counter after 37 minutes, Ramos tested visiting keeper Ivor Pandur with a decent drive from the edge of the box, before Jake Young fired a shot high over the bar.

In a sprightly start to the second half, with Kim showing some delightful touches around the St Mirren penalty area, Kelsy drove wide of the far post from 16 yards.

Then, in the 54th minute, Kim set up Kelsy but Chapman brilliantly deflected the close-range dink and the home side got the ball to safety before the stretching Kelsy could not connect properly with a cross from midfielder Nicolas Raskin.

However, the visitors eventually got the second when another swift attack ended with the ball coming out to Neil, whose shot came off St Mirren defender Louis Jackson and ended up in the back of the net.

St Mirren kept battling and Pandur made a terrific save from substitute Eseosa Sule’s strike from a Declan John cross.

The Rangers keeper then denied another St Mirren replacement, Luke Thomas, before Saints defender Calvin Ramsay headed against the outside of the post from the rebound, and that was effectively the end of St Mirren’ possible comeback.

Hoping to end their three-game winless run on Sunday, Aston Villa will travel to face struggling Premier League rivals Manchester United at Old Trafford.

#1894. MN: Furious Amorim gave long speech to Milan squad after Ferencvaros loss – the details

Ruben Amorim held a discussion with the team after the full-time whistle in the defeat to Ferencvaros, a report has claimed.

Milan lost 2-0 to the Hungarian side at San Siro last night, further complicating their Europa League campaign. The current table reads just three points earned in four games, which has seen the Rossoneri drop out of the top 24 spots.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

More worrying than the result was the team’s performance. The first-half showing was slow and laboured, but even when the big names came on in the second half, the team never gave the impression of being able to mount a comeback.

The sloppy goals conceded are a clear reflection of everything that went wrong, with individual errors and an attitude that’s hard to explain, especially after the resounding win against Inter in the derby just a few days ago.

According to MilanNews, Amorim gave a long speech to the team in the dressing room after the match. There was a face-to-face discussion about this disappointing defeat and how it came about, including the wrong approach and numerous shortcomings in the overall management of the match.

It came after Amorim had given his thoughts on the game to Sky, speaking about a lack of desire and concentration, and about how he could not defend a performance like that despite normally going to bat for his players. A response is needed in Genoa on Sunday, or it could be a bitter break.

In the changing room he held everyone – including himself – accountable. The Portuguese also touched on some points that have been reiterated cyclically by various coaches since the post-Scudetto season.

Among these is the fact that Milan carry greater responsibilities than other clubs and that wearing the Rossoneri shirt is not a prize, but rather a new step in everyone’s career. The reference to how Strahinja Pavlovic trains was emblematic in identifying the Serbian as the standard to follow.

Obviously, Gerry Cardinale also wasn’t happy with the defeat against Ferencvaros, which comes after the derby victory and four days of work that made it even more emotionally impactful. The Milan owner is expected to return to Italy for Genoa-Milan on Sunday, and intends to further investigate the team’s ups and downs.

#1893. Celtic star's telepathic connection with strike partner and why his best is yet to come

Callum Osmand continues to highlight his considerable potential by making his mark at Celtic, but the young forward is adamant that what supporters have witnessed so far is only the beginning.

The 20-year-old has experienced a whirlwind introduction to first-team football in Glasgow, with the demands of competing for a place at one of Scotland's biggest clubs providing a steep learning curve. Yet his decisive contribution to Celtic's dramatic 3-2 Europa League victory over Besiktas offered another glimpse of the qualities that have made him such an intriguing prospect.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Introduced by Martin O’Neill in the second half, Osmand wasted little time making his presence felt against the Turkish side, scoring just 43 seconds after coming on before delivering a perfectly weighted pass for Camilo Duran to complete his double. His impact transformed the contest and secured Celtic a much-needed victory.

“Yeah, it was crazy. It's a surreal feeling when it's my first touch as well,” he reflected. “I was a bit nervous that I'd shanked it, but no, I'm happy that I caught it nicely. He (O’Neill) knows that I know what he expects from me, so it was about making sure I can come and bring some energy.”

His burgeoning partnership with Duran was another highlight. Their understanding was evident in the build-up to Celtic's vital third goal, with the former Fulham forward displaying excellent vision to pick out the Colombian's run in behind.

“I thought he was offside, to be honest!” Osmand admitted. “I was looking at the bench saying 'Close?', and they were like, 'Yeah, it's tight', but I know where he's going. He's such a sharp striker, so I know if I put that in the space, the keeper is not getting anywhere near it. He's a top, top player, so I can't fault him at all.”

Their connection is extending beyond the pitch, too. Despite a language barrier, Osmand feels the pair have struck up a genuine friendship.

“His English is really not great, but somehow we manage to talk to each other a lot,” he laughed. “I think I find him quite a good friend of mine now. Although we might not speak many words, you can tell just by looking. We talk to each other a lot. Maybe it's little words, but we get on really well.

“Camilo is unbelievable, a really top player. You can see even by the way he walks and the way he moves. I learn off him every day. He's a great guy.”

The victory over Besiktas could prove pivotal to Celtic's European ambitions, and Osmand hopes it will provide the confidence required to approach the remaining fixtures with greater freedom.

“For us, it felt like a must-win. That was our mindset going into the game and it’s a huge result,” he explained. “We knew we could still qualify, but we knew we had to get something out of Thursday night, and I think the boys done amazing.

“Sometimes when you're not as confident, it's tough to play the football you want to play, but as you can see, when we're confident, it just goes forward every time. We know when we're not playing as well, and we'll be the first, as players, to critique each other and critique ourselves before anyone else. It is about just staying together, building and getting a result like this to take into the next game.”

Osmand is equally candid about his own development, insisting there is still plenty of room for improvement despite his encouraging start. He pointed out what will be key to taking his game to the next level.

“I'm nowhere near where I want to be personally, and there's stuff I need to tidy up on, like decision-making and all this stuff,” Osmand admitted. “But I feel like the more games I play, the more I understand and the more I learn. So on a personal note, that's what I want to do, just keep learning and keep understanding my role and obviously the players you're playing with.

“I've still only played a handful of games, so it's tough learning, but I feel like when you get thrown in the deep end, it's the best way to learn. It's just as long as I can get better every game, that's all I really want to focus on.”

His recent deployment on the left wing has also offered another opportunity to broaden his game. Although not a position he has traditionally occupied, Osmand is relishing the licence to express himself.

“I’m really enjoying it. It's a really fun position and it's very, very attacking,” he commented. “I have a lot of freedom and the staff give me that freedom and tell me to go and try and make something happen. It's a great feeling when you know you can just go and impose your game.”

#1892. ‘Different level’ – William Gallas backs Arsenal star for Real Madrid transfer

William Gallas believes that William Saliba could be tempted to join Real Madrid if the Spanish giants tried to sign the Arsenal defender.

Saliba joined Arsenal in a £27m move from Saint-Etienne in 2019 and has gone on to establish himself as one of the best centre-backs in the league.

The Frenchman was an integral part of Mikel Arteta’s side that won the league title last season, forming a rock-solid partnership with Gabriel Magalhaes at the heart of Arsenal’s defence.

Saliba is under contract at Arsenal until 2030, signing a long-term deal in 2025 after he was heavily linked with Real Madrid.

Sign up to our daily football newsletter, pick your team and get the latest news sent directly to your inbox every morning.

But Gallas still believes he is destined to play for Madrid, and said his fellow countryman would find it hard to turn down a move to a club of that stature.

‘Are Arsenal at a high enough level now that William Saliba would turn down Real Madrid if they came in for him?’ Gallas told SeatPick.

‘I know a lot of people will be mad about what I’m going to say right now but if we are talking about the history of both clubs, Real Madrid and Arsenal, then Real Madrid is Real Madrid. They are on a different level.’

‘The pressure is bigger there. The atmosphere around the club is different. Every game, the fans expect you to win. Every game, the fans expect you to have a great performance. Every season, the fans expect you to win La Liga or to win the Champions League, so it’s a different level.

‘For me, even if their performances at the moment are not the best, and even if they haven’t won the biggest trophies recently, Madrid is Madrid, and I’m telling you, any player who has the opportunity to go to Madrid, they will try to go there, and you can’t blame them. You couldn’t blame a player like Saliba if that is his decision.

‘Arsenal and Manchester United? They are still behind Barcelona and Real Madrid, even Manchester United still to this day because they have such a big history.

‘That’s why I think now with clubs like Arsenal, even if they had a good history in the past, what they are doing right now is rebuilding.

‘They are trying to tell their story again, and they are on the right track, but they are still behind Barcelona and Real Madrid.’

Saliba has not played a minute this campaign after suffering a back injury at the World Cup, but is now back in first-team training and closing in on a return.

Speaking recently about the Frenchman, Arteta said: ‘All the preparation has been done to measure all the loads and all the steps that he had to do to minimise that risk.

‘Now he’s in a really good place. He’s built the capacity that we needed, and now it’s about giving him minutes. He’s a centre-back, and when that’s the case, it’s not like an attacking midfielder or a nine that you can change.

‘A centre-back normally has to be able to play 90 minutes, and that’s why all the preparation that we’ve done to build him.’

Saliba was an unused substitute against Slavia Prague on Wednesday, but could be in line to feature against Hull City on Saturday after Ezri Konsa was forced off in the second half of their 2-1 win.

#1891. Saturday's Premier League predictions including Arsenal vs. Hull, Forest vs. Man City

By Ben Knapton | 07 Nov 2026 00:00

Today's Premier League predictions include champions Arsenal at home to Hull City, before challengers Manchester City take on Nottingham Forest.

A resurgent Tottenham Hotspur side travel to Elland Road to take on an out-of-sorts Leeds United outfit in the Premier League on Saturday lunchtime.

The spoils were shared the last time these two teams butted heads in May, with Mathys Tel’s opener cancelled out by a Dominic Calvert-Lewin penalty to rescue a 1-1 draw in North London.

Seven of Leeds’ nine Premier League matches this season have produced under 2.5 goals and we expected another tight affair against Tottenham this weekend.

The momentum is certainly with Spurs right now, but Leeds have made themselves difficult to beat at Elland Road and we can envisage the spoils being shared in a low-scoring draw on this occasion.

Two bottom-half Premier League teams battle it out at Craven Cottage on Saturday as Fulham play host to Newcastle United.

The Cottagers picked up all three points in their most recent meeting with the Magpies, securing a 2-0 home win in their final game of last season in May.

Newcastle supporters will be expecting a response of epic proportions from Jaissle’s side following a concerning run of form, but they come up against a Fulham outfit growing in confidence and resilience under Arbeloa.

None of the 18 Premier League meetings between these two teams in West London have ended all square (11 Fulham wins, seven Newcastle wins), but we believes that this run will come to an end with a low-scoring draw played out this weekend.

Seeking to open a six-point lead at the top of the Premier League table - for at least a couple of hours - Arsenal host Hull City at the Emirates Stadium in Saturday's 3pm mismatch.

The Gunners' statement win over Liverpool put them back in control of their title destiny, whereas the Tigers' winless run continued in gameweek nine with a 2-2 draw against Ipswich Town.

Hull in their 5-4-1 shape will do their utmost to frustrate Arsenal for as long as possible, but even a lightly fatigued Gunners side will find a way to break through eventually.

As the Tigers search for a response to no avail, Arteta's men should make the most of a more open contest, securing another straightforward win and extending their lead at the summit.

Second from bottom faces second from top in the Premier League on Saturday evening, as Nottingham Forest welcome Manchester City to the City Ground.

The two teams played out a 2-2 draw in their last meeting at the Etihad Stadium in March, with Elliot Anderson scoring a late equaliser for Forest before completing his big-money move to City in the summer.

Forest’s misfiring frontline is a growing concern for Glasner, but the hosts should take encouragement from Man City’s porous defence that has conceded 14 goals in their last seven games in all competitions.

A closely-contested battle could be in store this weekend, but we expect the Citizens to possess the clinical edge required to claim maximum points.

“I never thought things would turn out this way and that I would experience all this. Despite this, I want to send a message to our fans: they have been fantastic and we thank you so much for your support.

“We had our game plan. We prepared for every single eventuality. We knew that Amorim often changes formations and that in the last five or six games they have played with both three and four-man defences.

#1888. How football fanzines gave supporters a voice and changed the game forever

As has been evident once again during the opening months of the new season, Scottish football fans are not exactly slow to voice their displeasure or shy about agitating for change.

If they are unhappy with how their team is performing on the park or the way their club is being run off it, then they tend to make their feelings known.

Such activism is very much a modern-day phenomenon. So why do rabble-rousers stage protests in the streets, gather in angry mobs outside of stadiums, hold up inflammatory banners in the stands and boycott matches and merchandise when they are aggrieved about a perceived injustice?

Daniel Gray, the English author, editor of Scottish football quarterly Nutmeg and presenter of the When Saturday Comes podcast, believes the fanzine movement which reached its zenith in the 1980s and 1990s altered the landscape of the sport forever and ultimately emboldened the present-day supporter.

Gray’s fascination with fanzines – which can be traced back to the discarded copy of Fly Me To The Moon that he retrieved from the Ayresome Park terraces at a Middlesbrough match as an eight-year-old boy – has led to him penning a fascinating history of the independently produced publications which have long held him in thrall.

Fanzine: The Story of Football’s Alternative Press drives home how much professional football has changed, both for good and for ill, in the past five decades and underlines the role played in that transformation by those who grew frustrated at their voices not being heard during what was unquestionably a dark period in the game.

“Fanzines have led directly to so much of what we see going on in the sport today,” he said. “They were the first time that fans had ever spoken up for themselves. Before that, where and when did you ever hear from supporters?

“Maybe you got the odd letter in the local newspaper from time to time. But that would have been about it. There was never any criticism in the matchday programme. But finding a collective voice paved the way for what came next. It empowered fans.

“There was a definite reaction to fanzines. Clubs, politicians and the police were all terrified about having their authority questioned for the first time. Nobody would think twice about questioning the way the game is run now. There is a lineage back to fanzines in that.

“I am completely in awe of the people who were behind the whole fanzine movement. It would have been very easy for them to sit and moan and do nothing about the state of football in the 1980s. But they did something else altogether.”

Daniel Gray's new book Fanzine (Image: Promotional)

The Shamrock is widely considered to be the first football fanzine in the United Kingdom. It was a short-lived publication which John Doogan, a member of the Shamrock Celtic Supporters Club in Edinburgh, launched in 1963 due to his growing frustration at how poorly the Parkhead club was faring.

It contained poisonous attacks on the board and scathing analysis of the team and players, was sold outside the stadium on matchdays and became, much to the annoyance of the besieged hierarchy, popular due to the widespread disenchantment among the support.

Gray has seen a copy of the first edition which is held in the extensive fanzine archives in the National Library of Scotland in the capital. He is firmly of the opinion it is as important a tome as its prized copy of the Gutenberg Bible. “It is quite something,” he said. “It is up there with all of their ancient relics for me.”

It was, though, a different era that he was most interested in. Fanzine focuses on a turbulent time of seismic change in British football.

“I honed in on the 10-year period between the mid-1980s, when the fanzine boom really started, and the mid-1990s, when modern football, in inverted commas, came into being,” he said.

“I came across research which claimed, and it was a conservative estimate, that a million fanzines were sold in the 1980s and 1990s. It became this mass movement. I wanted to tell the story of that movement, but also to tell the story of that time in football through the eyes of the fans.

“I wanted to show what fans were thinking about and feeling. I knew the conditions fans experienced when they went to a match were bad, but I didn't realise quite how bad until I started to go through those thousands of fanzines. There is a lot of stuff about how fans were treated by the police and how unsafe a lot of the grounds were.

“The public perception of football fans was just so bad. The perception was that all fans were hooligans. Fanzines came about to show that was untrue, to show that a lot of fans were funny and bright and talked about music and politics and books and other things. They really did reshape the way the fans were perceived.”

Gray added, “One of the greatest agonies of going through all of these old fanzines was seeing how prescient many of the writers were. A lot of them were saying grounds were inherently unsafe, a lot of them were warning that bad things were going to happen.

“Sure enough, there were then these big, horrible events, the disasters at Bradford, at Heysel and at Hillsborough. It was far, far worse than anyone could possibly have imagined.

Meadowbank Thistle fanzine AWOL (Image: Promotional)

“So their writing was incredibly perceptive. The quality of the writing, the campaigning and the solidarity between them all helped to change both the way fans were viewed and the conditions in which they watched matches.

“In the mid-1980s, you didn't admit you were a football fan in polite company. By the early 1990s, television networks and radio stations were desperate to have fan-based content. Celebrities, too, were trying to attach themselves to football. A lot changed in a short journey.”

But it was the edgy, often bizarre, frequently hilarious humour in the fanzines which Gray, and so many football supporters of his vintage, adored. He found himself in stitches as he perused the pages of beloved Scottish titles like AWOL, the fabled Meadowbank Thistle publication which is highly prized by collectors.

“I came across an Arbroath fanzine from the late 1980s called Tomato Soup and Lentils in the National Library archives," he said. "It had a bit of the Brechin hedge sellotaped to it. It was a free gift.

“I spoke to Archie MacGregor of the marvellous The Absolute Game and he felt that Scottish fanzines were different from English fanzines and perhaps had more humour in them because fans up here in Scotland weren't faced with as many obstacles as fans in England were. ID cards, for example, were being threatened down south at one point.

“So the tone was slightly different here in Scotland, there was probably a bit more room for sarcasm. They were very sardonic and quite surreal at times. They were far more earnest in England.

“Generally speaking, the lower down the leagues the club was, the better the fanzine it had. There was far more for their fans to moan about so it made for much better content. So the St Mirren and Dundee United fanzines would tend to have a far higher level of sarcasm.

“Meadowbank Thistle had a strangely large number of fanzines for such a small club. AWOL was utterly fantastic. It is loved by a lot of people. There was some football content, but on the whole they wrote about other things.

“They once had an article that was headlined 'The Shoplifter’s Guide to Edinburgh'. That was a bit too much for the club and those responsible got hauled in to answer some questions. But that was fairly typical of the strand of Scottish humour that ran through fanzines. There was definitely surrealism.”

The origin stories of the titles, which include Brian Moore's Head Looks Uncannily Like London Planetarium (Gillingham), The Deranged Ferret (Lincoln City), The Memoirs of Seth Bottomley (Port Vale) and 53 Miles West of Venus (Preston North End), were often as funny as the stories contained within.

A fanzine seller at Turf Moor (Image: Phil Oldham / Shutterstock)

Gray particularly liked Wendy Who?, which St Johnstone fans named after a song they regularly belted out during matches at their old Muirton Park home.

"Oh Wendy Saints, oh Wendy Saints, oh Wendy Saints go marching in . . . "

“I loved a Dundee United fanzine called Can I Bring My Dog?," said Gray. "It was a question a United fan asked the organiser of a supporters' bus before a trip to Denmark for a European game. I thought that was brilliant.

“There’s A Store Where the Creatures Meet was a St Mirren fanzine which the author Christopher Brookmyre wrote for. Those are the lyrics from The Doors’ song Love Street, which was obviously the name of their old ground.

“The crossover between music magazines and football fanzines was huge. Quite often when I was going through old fanzines a flexi-disc would fall out."

Gray continued, “Very creative people got involved during what was a really energising time in football. There was an awful lot of quality writing, including by people like Christopher Brookmyre, Irvine Welsh and Neil Forsyth.

“The first time Neil saw his words in print was in a Dundee United fanzine. Irvine wrote for Hibs fanzines under various pseudonyms. He probably cut his teeth writing for Hibs Monthly in the late 1980s. Anyone could send something in. There was a wonderful democracy to it.”

Internet message boards, social media websites and short-form video platforms are the outlets which football supporters use to vent their spleens in 2026. The digital age, though, has by no means brought about an end to fanzines. Indeed, Gray found they are enjoying something of a revival.

“There are around 70 printed fanzines still left,” he said. “A lot of them are old titles like Fly Me To The Moon at Middlesbrough, A Love Supreme at Sunderland and The City Gent at Bradford. But there are new fanzines which younger supporters are producing as well.

“I am sensing a real desire to get away from screens and to embrace this very old medium. I think football supporters love having something ephemeral. They love an object that marks them being at a match.

“Few clubs use physical tickets now and fewer clubs are producing matchday programmes now. So maybe fanzines are becoming your souvenir of the day, of the game.

“It has been a bit unexpected, but it is happening. I see a real interest in getting away from the anger and the hot air of YouTube channels, social media sites and radio phone-ins and a desire to just be a bit more reflective.

A Manchester United fanzine seller at Old Trafford (Image: Philip Oldham/BPI / Shutterstock)

“I don't think there's going to be a full-scale renaissance or a return to what the movement once was. It is similar to the rise in popularity of vinyl records among music lovers, which nobody saw coming. I do feel there is a space for them, a role for them.

“I certainly yearn for the fanzine, for the content that was in them and for the tone of them. So much football writing now is about tactics and transfers. I miss something that is barely relevant to the match I was at, that is full of humour and that reflects what fans actually talk about when they stand behind the goal.

“Yes, the 1980s was undoubtedly a horrific time to watch football. But there were elements to it, like the affordability that went out the window, in the Premier League anyway, when all-seater stadiums came in during the early 1990s, that I do miss.”

Fanzine was a real labour of love for Gray and it shows. It is a forensically detailed, beautifully crafted, utterly engrossing account of the glorious heyday of the often bonkers but invariably brilliant magazines which football fanatics who were determined to have their say produced in their bedrooms, in their garden sheds and on their kitchen tables.

There is, with Scottish magazines like Cappielow Bugle (Morton), Follow Follow (Rangers), Northern Light (Aberdeen), Not The View (Celtic), Railway Ender (Ayr United) and Walking Down The Halbeath Road (Dunfermline) covered, plenty of interest for fans from these shores.

“It was a privilege to write it,” he said. “The sort of person who started a fanzine wasn't really in it for an ego trip or to further their career. Sometimes it takes an outsider like me to say, ‘What you did was incredible’.”

Fanzine: The Story of Football’s Alternative Press by Daniel Gray is published by Bloomsbury Sport, costs £20, and is available to buy now.

Newcastle United defender Amar Dedic sparked a major police operation after he was spotted carrying a bow and arrows near a reservoir in Northumberland.

Dedic, who joined Newcastle in a £30 million deal from Benfica in the summer, was reported by a member of the public who saw him and a friend walking with the weapon near the small village of Harlow Hill.

#1885. Wolves loanee has no regrets about rocky Celtic ride as he steps out of shadows to embrace the spotlight

Sam Johnstone has experienced enough of football's highs and lows to understand that joining Celtic was never likely to be a straightforward undertaking.

But despite a turbulent introduction to life in Glasgow, the Wolves loanee insists he has absolutely no regrets about taking on one of the most demanding challenges of his career to date.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

The former England international headed north of the border earlier this summer in search of regular first-team football and a fresh challenge. What followed has been a mixed introduction, with inconsistent results bringing added scrutiny, while adapting to a new team environment has required patience.

His career has been defined as much by patience as it has by perseverance. The Manchester United youth product has spent lengthy spells waiting in the wings for his opportunity, often occupying a back-up or third-choice role, while striving to establish himself as a No.1

Arriving at Celtic has offered a welcome change of circumstances. Rather than being confined to a supporting role, Johnstone has the chance to make the position between the sticks his own as he continues to enjoy a sustained run of games and remind people of the qualities that once earned him international recognition.

There is also the matter of developing relationships with the defenders in front of him. Communication, trust and familiarity are essential for any goalkeeper, and Johnstone recognises that those connections take time to establish.

“I think I've got to get used to them, they've got to get used to me, and that only happens through playing and through games. It's great to be in the team,” he said. “To get a run of games for any player, you find your rhythm. It was a new club for me, a new team, so that takes probably a couple of games to get used to as well.”

Having represented established clubs such as West Bromwich Albion and Crystal Palace, Johnstone is no stranger to pressure. However, he has discovered that the expectations at Celtic are particularly intense, arguably unlike anything he has experienced elsewhere in his career.

“Of course it has,” Johnstone admitted when asked whether fluctuating results had affected the mood within the dressing room. “I think the results affect it. This club's not used to losing, and we've probably lost too many games for this club.

“The expectation here, rightly so, is to win. Unfortunately, we hadn't quite met that expectation, and the lads know that. We all realise that, but we have to put things right in each game. It was tough. We're honest players, we're honest people, and honest with each other.”

Ultimately, though, signing for Celtic was an opportunity Johnstone was never likely to pass up. The quality within Martin O’Neill’s squad, coupled with the passion of the supporters and the chance to experience the club's unique atmosphere, made the move an attractive proposition.

“It's brilliant to play for this club,” he insisted. “The passion of the fans, good and bad. The standard of players on the pitch, day in, day out at training. When I came, I said I didn't have to think twice about coming here. It’s a great team to play in. The lads came up with the goods (on Thursday vs Besiktas], so we keep taking it game by game and go again on Sunday.”

Whether his time with the Scottish champions will provide the springboard to revitalise his career remains to be seen. Asked if the move had given him a fresh lease of life, Johnstone was typically measured in his response. “Let's see, let's see.”

#1883. Why Unai Emery is right to turn down Manchester United and stick with Aston Villa

It’s a great quirk of Premier League scheduling that Manchester United welcome Aston Villa to Old Trafford this weekend, after a week in which Jamie Carragher’s suggestion that Villa manager Unai Emery would jump at the chance to move to United prompted a legal threat from the midlands club, an apology from the outspoken pundit and an announcement late on Wednesday that Emery and his bosses had ‘positive discussions establishing a clear commitment beyond 2029 for the joint development of the club’.

A new contract is reportedly imminent for the Spaniard, and who could possibly blame Emery for sticking around at a club that have repeatedly backed him, given him more control than he’ll have anywhere else and whose fans worship him for delivering their first trophy in 30 years last season.

The alternative? Joining a constant catastrophe that everyone agrees needs far more than just a new manager to put back together.

Sign up to our daily football newsletter, pick your team and get the latest news sent directly to your inbox every morning.

While Emery is going nowhere, the whole affair does raise questions about football’s food chain, something which definitely does exist but is clearly going through some changes right now.

Managers will always believe they are the right person to take a once great club and bring back the glory days, and being the one to do so is an intoxicating idea.

But Emery has been here before and was burned by his experience at Arsenal where a collection of expensive failed transfers and unmotivated senior players gave him the worst possible platform to build from. Sound familiar?

All roads still lead to Real Madrid for players but the money involved in Premier League football means simply being a relatively successful English club puts you closer to the top of the chain than ever before, and given United’s penchant for finding new lows every season, a move from Villa north to Manchester is at best a sideways move these days – just ask Youri Tielemans.

Also, given the relative state of flux that many of the ‘big six’ find themselves in these days, there’s an opportunity for Emery and Villa to elbow their way in and become a more established fixture towards the top of the league.

Select your team for football news tailored to you Close

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

United are joined by Spurs in their ability to self-implode, Chelsea are chaotic at the best of times, Liverpool are still just about managing the transition to a Jurgen Klopp-less existence and Manchester City are unlikely to be challenging for titles in the near future, depending on impending sanctions.

Only Arsenal are properly set up for consistent success, and Villa clearly believe trusting in Emery is the best way to eventually get themselves into the title conversation.

There are pitfalls to their approach – if Emery does someday get his head turned by a massive paycheck in Saudi Arabia or Real Madrid do come calling, he may still move on and leave the club as a ship without a sail, which is why clubs like Brighton and Brentford treat their managers as cogs in a well-oiled system.

United fans had some temporary relief midweek with their emotional comeback against Roma in the Champions League and may well go into the international break feeling good if they manage to squeeze out a win on Sunday, but regardless of the result, Emery is in the right place.

#1882. Rangers turn up heat on leaders Celtic despite controversy in Paisley

A bitterly cold, damp Saturday night in Paisley yielded precisely the sort of calculated, business-like victory that defines title credentials. Under the floodlights of the Marbill Coaches Stadium, Rangers maintained their pursuit of league leaders Celtic with a dominant 2-0 win over St Mirren.

In truth, the scoreline scarcely reflected the visitors’ control of proceedings, a superiority anchored by a dominant midfield display and punctuated by goals from Ryan Naderi and Dan Neil in either half.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

This was an exercise in efficiency for Rangers manager Derek McInnes as his side arrived in Renfrewshire looking to maintain their unbeaten away record in the league this season. Making just one change from last weekend’s Premier Sports Cup semi-final triumph over Aberdeen, his side displayed a fluid composure that left the hosts chasing shadows for long periods.

Although Rangers have endured an inconsistent record on previous visits to Paisley, dropping points in three of their last four league outings, their latest success extended a domestic unbeaten run to 12 matches and left them in a confident place heading into the final international break of the year.

St Mirren, under the stewardship of Craig McLeish, had promised a robust, positive approach as they looked to arrest a worrying slide in form that had saw them lose six of their previous eight games. However, the reality for the Buddies was an evening spent largely in a low defensive block, starved of possession and unable to test Ivor Pandur in the visitors' goal until it was too late.

The breakthrough arrived in the 18th minute through a moment of controversy. Left-back James Penrice drove into the penalty area and went down under pressure from a trailing Samuel Ramos leg. While the home support vociferously claimed the new Scotland call-up went down theatrically, referee Nick Walsh pointed directly to the spot.

Naderi stepped forward, ignored the jeers, and showed admirable composure to confidently dispatch the penalty into the bottom right-hand corner, with Jacob Chapman diving the opposite direction. It marked the German’s sixth goal in his last seven games.

Going behind did little to alter St Mirren’s conservative shape as their build-up play lacked urgency, and Rangers continued to dictate the tempo. Their front three of Badredine Bouanani, Kim Minsu, and Kevin Kelsy probed intelligently. The hosts did have a penalty appeal of their own dismissed when Ramos’ header back across goal appeared to strike Naderi’s hand.

The second half followed an identical script, and the definitive blow arrived just after the hour mark. It was a goal engineered by the persistent work of Kelsy who battled fiercely to pick up Olwethu Makhanya’s pass.

His determination allowed the ball to break kindly to Neil, restored to the starting line-up, on the edge of the box and the midfielder side-footed effort took a wicked deflection of Declan John to completely wrong-foot the helpless Chapman, with the ball nestling in the bottom left-hand corner. It gave Rangers some welcome breathing room.

St Mirren did mount a late, spirited assault on the visitors goal, but were denied on several occasions by Pandur. Their best opportunity fell to substitute Eseosa Sule, who met a pinpoint cross from John at the back post. It seemed a certain goal, but the Croatian goalkeeper produced a sublime reaction save to preserve his clean sheet.

Ultimately, McInnes’s men navigated the closing stages with a minimum of fuss, starving the hosts of the ball and suffocating any remaining glimmers of a late comeback. The victory keeps them firmly within striking distance at the summit, a solitary point behind reigning champions Celtic with a game in hand still to play after this weekend.

#1881. Saturday's Serie A predictions including Roma vs. Sassuolo, Parma vs. Bologna

By Darren Plant | 07 Nov 2026 00:00, Last updated: 07 Nov 2026 00:00

Today's Serie A predictions include the showdown between Roma and Sassuolo at Stadio Olimpico, as well as Parma hosting Bologna.

Both beaten again last week, Torino and Lecce will look to end their losing streaks when they meet each other on Saturday.

While Toro have just suffered back-to-back defeats, their visitors are also sliding down the Serie A standings.

Although Torino have been leaking too many goals, they possess more attacking thrust than their limited visitors.

Since April, Lecce have gone 14 league games without a draw, and that streak will continue with their fourth straight defeat.

Winless at Cagliari since 2013, Frosinone head into Saturday's gameweek-11 fixture at Unipol Domus as the likely favourites.

The promoted side have thrived since returning to the top flight, sitting sixth in the Serie A table ahead of another visit to a ground where they have not won in over a decade.

Raimondo's absence removes a significant source of goals for Frosinone, but Birligea's recent brace against Lecce suggests that the visitors retain enough firepower to trouble their struggling hosts.

#1878. Arsenal urged to avoid £64m transfer mistake after Micah Richards claim

Arsenal should be wary of selling Viktor Gyokeres in the January transfer window, according to former Gunners striker Jeremie Aliadiere.

Gyokeres produced his best performance of the season in midweek with a goal and an assist to help the Gunners beat Slavia Prague 2-1 in the Champions League.

But it has otherwise proved to be a frustrating few months for the Swede, who has started just one Premier League match for Mikel Arteta’s side so far this season.

Gyokeres amassed a respectable 21 goals in all competitions in his maiden season after arriving from Sporting CP for £64million, but now faces an uncertain future at the Emirates having fallen beneath Kai Havertz in the pecking order.

Sign up to our daily football newsletter, pick your team and get the latest news sent directly to your inbox every morning.

With speculation likely to mount ahead of the January window, some pundits, including Micah Richards, have suggested that the Gunners should look to move Gyokeres on.

But former Arsenal striker Aliadiere believes that might be a mistake and ultimately leave Arteta short of options at the top of the pitch.

‘I think it’s all depending on the finances how much they can get for him and who to replace him with,’ Aliadiere told Metro.

‘Because I think as much as obviously he’s not in the top 11 now because Havertz is preferred number one, you don’t want to sell him, get a good price and not be able to replace him.

‘If Havertz gets injured, which obviously we’ve seen in the past – he’s had a few injuries and he can pick up injuries – you just end up with no striker at all.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

‘So I think it’s a very difficult January transfer window. Do you try to buy someone before you sell? I think when you look over the summer, selling Trossard and Martinelli before buying somebody.

‘Obviously, they go to Tzolis, but I’m not sure Tzolis was bought to be the first choice and when he is injured, you end up doing Eze on the left-hand side, and that’s not really his best position in my opinion.

‘So I don’t want it to happen with Gyokeres, thinking let’s try to sell him and recuperate a good transfer fee for him and then not replacing him.’

But even if Gyokeres remains at the club, Aliadiere can’t envisage the 28-year-old becoming the long-term solution to Arsenal’s search for a clinical striker.

‘I just feel the way Arsenal plays does not quite suit Gyokeres’ style of play,’ Aliadiere, speaking via football betting, added.

‘I’ve always been very quite patient and looking at the good stuff that he does, and I still feel that he does some amazing work. But I just do feel that the players don’t really give him the ball quick enough, which is what he needs.

‘He needs to be on 1v1. He needs to run the channel, get fed the ball quite quickly. And I feel we’re not really playing that way. We like to control the ball.

‘We like to control the tempo and just slow down the game. And I just feel Gyokeres is more of a counter-attacking player where he sees the space, he wants it quickly and then he’s on 1v1 and then he can then dominate physically.

‘But he’s rarely getting in that position, so I just find it difficult to kind of see him turning things around in a way of probably just being a rotation player.’

#1876. Derek McInnes pinpoints Rangers biggest strength as St Mirren fume over penalty award and VAR consistency

Derek McInnes insists Rangers are heading in the right direction after extending their unbeaten domestic run to 12 matches with a comfortable 2-0 victory over St Mirren in Paisley.

Goals in either half from Ryan Naderi and captain Dan Neil secured another valuable three points for the Ibrox side, who moved to within a point of league leaders Celtic, with a game in hand still to play after this weekend.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Despite acknowledging that his team could have been more clinical in front of goal, McInnes was delighted with the way his players approached what he considers one of the more difficult away assignments in the Scottish Premiership.

“I think this is a hard place to come for any team, but for our club as well, over the years it's never easy and we didn't expect it to be anything other than that,” McInnes said. “But I thought we dealt with the game really well. I thought we were really competitive from the get-go, I thought we were tenacious, we were aggressive, we moved the ball right.

“We just came back to that last part of it not being clinical enough. Quite ironic, we scored two goals tonight from a penalty kick and a deflected shot at the edge of the box, given all the chances we had, but I actually thought in the main it was no more than we deserved.”

Naderi was once again central to Rangers' attacking efforts, taking his season's tally to nine goals and five assists after confidently dispatching his first-half spot-kick.

McInnes was particularly impressed by the striker's work rate and physical presence, believing the forward has taken significant strides in recent weeks as he looks to establish himself as a dependable option to lead the line.

“I think he's so willing. His first port of call was to make sure he's a handful to play against and I thought he was that,” McInnes stated. “He needs to build that reputation for being horrible to play against, but equally at a club like Rangers you're going to get judged on the goals.

“He's totally shown that he's somebody you can depend on, somebody that can be trusted, somebody that you can rely on to get goals as well as bring in good performances.”

McInnes was equally thrilled with goalkeeper Ivor Pandur, who produced several important saves to preserve Rangers' clean sheet as St Mirren threatened a comeback in the closing stages.

“I think he's been very clean, very controlled with what he does. His distribution is brilliant, he makes good decisions,” he said. “I think there's so much potential in Ivor. With a rotten goalie, you're not winning nothing. He is somebody who we really take a lot of comfort from.

“I've played with goalkeepers who were brilliant and I've played with some who weren't so good and you never ever felt comfortable. With him, we do. He's been a big part of the amount of clean sheets we've had. I thought we worked hard for a clean sheet tonight but there was a spell in the second half where the space got a wee bit bigger and St Mirren managed to get a few opportunities. Thankfully, you always feel he's got that save in him.”

St Mirren have one win from their last nine league games and boss Craig McLeish was left frustrated by the first-half penalty award, questioning the consistency of the decisions made by officials following Samuel Ramos’ challenge on James Penrice.

“My thoughts on the penalty... If that's the criteria for contact in the box, then fine,” he said. “But Kabs [Ismeal Kabia] gets wiped out in the second half after he puts a cross in. I don't even know if anyone looks at it.

“We get an apology after the game at Ibrox for a penalty that we should have got on Kabs again where there was a decent amount of contact on it. I get that if the ref gives it on the field, then it's maybe difficult for VAR to overturn it. I think if he doesn't give it there and then, I don't think VAR gets involved to give it.

“It's a difficult one and it's a frustrating one from our point of view, but there's also bits leading up to it getting to that situation that we need to deal with better. I need to be careful with what I'm saying. It's a frustrating one from our point of view.”

Asked whether he had spoken to Nick Walsh after the final whistle to seek clarification, McLeish replied bluntly: “No, there's no point.”

#1874. Leeds United 1 Spurs 0: Okafor the hero as intense, in-character second half ends winless streak

Shortly after being serenaded after coming on in the final quarter at Elland Road, he took care of Spurs in the here and now.

The fact that three substitutes all combined will not have been missed by Daniel Farke, who misses nothing.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

A throw-in from Melvin Bard was won by Dominic Calvert-Lewin with the ball dropping to Harry Wilson, who had the presence of mind to spot Okafor, who gave Rodrigo Bentacur the slip before firing home confidently on 77 minutes.

And that was that as Leeds produced an intense, in-character second half to secure a first win in six matches and head into the international break in improved mood. A fourth win in a row for the first time in over 1,000 days continues for Spurs.

The win was not without controversy, that said.

It took a big moment on 37 minutes to set pulses truly racing among home punters in an otherwise pretty uneventful first half.

A lengthy VAR check saw the Stockley Park overlords scrutinise Jayden Bogle’s challenge on Mathys Tel for a considerable length of time before it was deemed not to be serious foul play.

Tel was left writhing in agony after being caught on the back of his Achilles by Bogle’s left foot. It looked accidental as opposed to intentional and the video decision-makers concurred, although it could easily have gone the other way and resulted in a red card.

Tel managed to carry on for a few minutes before eventually making way.

The other incident of note also involved technology with an early check resulting in a non-penalty award for Leeds after a cross caught Mateus Fernandes’ shoulder. The Spurs midfielder’s arm was outstretched, but it was rightly deemed as not intentional.

Headline team news from a home perspective saw Lucas Nmecha and Longstaff handed first league starts of the campaign, with Harry Wilson and Dan James dropping to the bench.

You had to go back to last November for the previous time that Longstaff stepped out from the off at Premier League level.

Spurs-wise, ex-United favourite Archie Gray switched to midfield following the recall of Pedro Porro at right-back.

Gray received a few jeers whenever he touched the ball. Spurs had some half-decent moments in transition and had the better of it in open play and more control - with Fernandes seeing plenty of the ball in particular. Leeds displayed perspiration, but little inspiration.

Spurs’ best moments arrived midway through the half. An incisive move down Leeds’ right ended in Omar Marmoush’s low shot taking a slight, but important touch off Tarik Muharemovic before James Trafford gathered. The deflection took the sting out of it.

Mohammed Kudus also tested Trafford low down, with the Leeds keeper having no first-half dramas unlike seven days earlier.

Leeds, who started nicely enough, huffed and puffed. One chance arrived ahead of the break but Nmecha’s downward header was easily claimed by Antonin Kinsky.

Leeds made a change at the interval, with Melvin Bard coming on for Gabriel Gudmundsson, presumably due to an injury concern.

Attacking the Kop, Leeds produced a dangerous moment with Van de Ven getting a key clearance in front of goal after Bogle whipped in an excellent low centre.

Longstaff’s left-wing corner yielded the hosts best moment up to press.

Calvert-Lewin directed a header towards goal and Dominic Solanke got an important block. The Leeds striker helped the ball back into the danger zone, with Nico Elvedi nodding wide.

United, attacking the Kop, were starting to up it and soon missed a golden chance after Tanaka and Longstaff led the break.

Calvert-Lewin did well to evade van der Veen and teed up Tanaka, who ballooned an excellent chance over.

Nevertheless, Leeds were the ones in the ascendancy and Spurs were starting to look flustered all of a sudden. Indicative of that was a triple change just before the midway point of the half from Roberto De Zerbi.

One flash of life - in relative isolation -from the visitors saw one of the substitutes in Conor Gallagher fire a shot just wide. Most of the action was towards the other end. Nmecha hit a post, but the flag was instantly raised before Calvert-Lewin fired over, soon followed by Bogle.

Leeds continued to knock on the door, with Kinsky forced into significant work to tip over Longstaff’s hooked effort in splendid fashion.

The pressure was sustained and the Kop sucked one in. Trafford made a key late save to deny Van Hecke.

#1873. Why Jobe Bellingham received England call-up instead of Kobbie Mainoo

Jobe Bellingham has been given his first England call-up with Thomas Tuchel claiming Kobbie Mainoo’s recent injury problems cost him a place in the latest squad.

The Borussia Dortmund midfielder will join his brother Jude for Nations League games against Croatia and Spain having impressed Tuchel and his staff this season.

He joins James Garner, Elliot Anderson, Declan Rice and Myles Lewis-Skelly as Tuchel’s central midfield options with Manchester United star Mainoo among the list of high profile absentees which once again includes Cole Palmer and Phil Foden.

Mainoo was part of England’s World Cup squad but did not play a single minute. He was included in the group for the extended international break in September and October but was among a spate of injury withdrawals.

Sign up to our daily football newsletter, pick your team and get the latest news sent directly to your inbox every morning.

Mainoo has been first choice in midfield under Michael Carrick when available, missing four of his side’s 14 games through injury. He returned to the team against Chelsea last weekend before playing a key role in the midweek victory over Roma.

Speaking on Friday, Tuchel said Mainoo’s injury last month was a key reason behind the decision not to select him with Jobe getting the nod instead.

‘I think Kobbie has had a difficult spell and missed a lot of matches,’ Tuchel said. ‘In the meantime it was Jobe who impressed in the same level of time and that is what we want.

#1869. Daniel Farke on 'spot-on' Leeds United, Noah Okafor admission, Gabriel Gudmundsson update + on Spurs controversy

An outstanding second half culminated in a deserved winner in the 77th minute from substitute Noah Okafor, with fellow replacements Harry Wilson and Melvin Bard also contributing to the goal. Okafor scored with his second touch.

It was a merited three points for Leeds, who mustered 13 goal attempts on the restart.

Did you know with a Digital subscription to Yorkshire Post, you can get access to all of our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Farke said: "There's no replacement for this winning feeling after such a game in the dressing room. It's great to have this winning feeling back.

"All the credit and all my compliments go to the boys' terrific performance against a really in-form Tottenham side.

"You could see in the first half that they would go with confidence also into this game. For us, of course, a difficult period because we're missing - since a few weeks more or less - in training and also in the starting line-ups, some key players like Anton Stach, Noah Okafor and for Dominic (Calvert-Lewin). It’s not the easiest spell with several injury problems.

"It was important today to show this unity and commitment. We were technically spot on in order to avoid all their processes and all their individual quality in order to score goals and reduce them to very, very little already in the first half.

"We were missing a bit in our game (in the first half) in our final third was again the quality of the crosses and the finishing pass was perhaps not there, but I think in the second half there was no doubt just one team was pushing."

On the impact of Okafor, who had been struggling with an abductor issue, he continued: "Credit to our medical department and also to Noah, he has worked in a very, very disciplined fashion, 24 hours a day more or less to be available.

"Yesterday with a few concerns of the medical department, they said: 'Boss, Listen, if you want to use him, you have to make sure that you stay unbelievably disciplined and you can't bring him on longer than 15 or 20 minutes, this is what the muscle can't handle (more minutes). But if you want to do this and Noah feels also right, then yeah, perhaps you can do this.' He took part yesterday in parts of our team training."

Farke confirmed that Swedish international Gabriel Gudmundsson came off with a hamstring injury at the break, with Bard coming on and performing excellently in his place.

He said: "Gaby had problems with his hamstring, so it was not possible for him to keep going. I always prefer to have Gabby available but don't get me wrong, but I had a good feeling straight away because Melvin had his best week in training since he was together with us.

"He could feel that he has momentum and I was not for one moment concerned when I had to throw him in. I hope that it's not too bad with Gaby and I hope to have him back on the other side of the international break, but also credit for Melvin.

The win was not without controversy, that said.

It took a big moment on 37 minutes to set pulses truly racing among home punters in an otherwise pretty uneventful first half.

A lengthy VAR check saw the Stockley Park overlords scrutinise Jayden Bogle’s challenge on Mathys Tel for a considerable length of time before it was deemed not to be serious foul play.

Tel was left writhing in agony after being caught on the back of his Achilles by Bogle’s left foot. It looked accidental as opposed to intentional and the video decision-makers concurred, although it could easily have gone the other way and resulted in a red card.

Tel managed to carry on for a few minutes before eventually making way. He left the stadium on crutches after the game.

Farke said: "I haven't watched the scenes back and didn't have the chance, so for that I can't give a clear opinion on it. I would need to watch it back. The scene with Jayden was not too far away from my bench, I think it looked a bit like a very unlucky coming together.

"Of course sadly for Mathys that he was injured, and of course fingers crossed that he's back pretty soon. But it felt a bit like there was not too much speed in this action, and what I can guarantee is Jayden Bogle is one of the most fair players in the whole country.

"He's too much sometimes for me like a butterfly and not like an eagle anyhow, so soft in a positive way. What I can guarantee is that he would never ever injure a player on purpose, or not even foul a player on purpose, because he's a great character."

Spurs chief Roberto De Zerbi had no complaints about the result and felt his side's second-half performance lacked 'personality'.

He said: "It was two games in the same game. In the first half, we had clear chances to score and didn't suffer.

"In the second half, I don't know why, we suffered too much and deserved to lose game. We didn't win any duels and one-on-one's. There was space to play, but we didn't take the right positions and didn't show personality and who we are.

"I don't want excuses. We have to be honest, if we are not honest today, the future is not good. I was surprised as my players worked very well this week. We spoke all week about the intensity and type of game we would find in this stadium. It was not a surprise for us."

On the incident regarding Tel, he added: "I can't say something more because I didn't clearly see the situation.

"I was surprised, because in the same position in the second half, there were two different fouls and two yellow cards (offences) on Pedro Porro.

"I don't know if it was a red card or not on Mathys Tel, but for sure Pedro Porro, it was a yellow card. Why I'm telling it like this, because the parameter of the referee was not good enough, I think, for these both situations."
